newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Brass band keeps dying mining village alive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Brass band keeps dying mining village alive.

text.p: It is five years since the coalmine closed in Grimethorpe, depriving the Yorkshire town of its main industry and hundreds of people of their livelihoods.
But the colliery's brass band is thriving.
Since the Grimethorpe Colliery Band starred in the hit film, "Brassed Off", it has been inundated with requests for television appearances and its concerts are sellouts.
"We've really come to the fore," said Ken Hirst, the band's secretary for the past 43 years.
"Brassed Off" is set in the fictional town of "Grimey", but it was filmed among Grimethorpe's red-brick miners' houses and its tale is a familiar one in this northern English town.
The year is 1992 and "Grimey's" pit is threatened with closure, just as the colliery's band has won a place at the national brass band championships.
Grimethorpe's colliery closed at the beginning of 1993, just four days before the colliery band won the national championship with 199 points out of 200.
PIT CLOSURES BROUGHT HARDSHIP

It was a time of deep gloom in Britain's coal mining towns. The miners had lost a long and bloody battle with the government against pit closures. A year-long strike in 1984 had left them destitute and humiliated.
Grimethorpe has never recovered. The litter-strewn high street is dotted with boarded-up shops and there is a gaping wasteland where the colliery used to be.
"Brassed Off's" star Tara Fitzgerald won few friends when she reportedly described Grimethorpe as the "arsehole to nowhere". But the casual visitor can see what she means.
The town is little more than a few rows of houses on a scrubby, potholed loop of road off the main route between Barnsley and Pontefract.

Even in the bright sunshine of a February day it feels desolate. The only people about are one or two disconsolate-looking dogwalkers and curtains of many of the houses are drawn against the sunlight.
The town's saving grace is its colliery band, whose music provides a stirring background to "Brassed Off".

The players may be amateurs -- traditionally they were mineworkers -- but the band is highly respected in the music world. Britain's top composers, including Harrison Birtwhistle, have written music specially for them.
WELL-KNOWN BANDS ATTRACT SPONSORSHIP

As in the film, northern England's traditional colliery bands faced a grim future when the pits closed. Many broke up, although some of the more famous ones like Grimethorpe managed to struggle by with private sponsorship.
RJB Mining Plc which bought all the surviving English coalmines when they were privatised in 1994 has promised to sponsor the Grimethorpe band until 1998.

But the cosy old relationship with the mine owners was lost. The National Coal Board enjoyed the prestige the bands brought, and allowed the players time off to practice and perform. Hirst was transferred to his job from the Coal Board's management.

The Grimethorpe Colliery Band was founded in 1917 by players from Grimethorpe and the neighbouring village of Cudworth who worked in the mine. They persuaded the colliery, then privately-owned, to sponsor them.
Now only one band member actually lives in Grimethorpe and none are miners. Those who do have jobs have to juggle their work with their commitments to the band.
"It is hard at times, especially in the last few months when we've been so busy," said Richard Marshall, the band's youthful principal cornet player.
Marshall, a music student, was poached from a rival band last year. "It was a dream come true," he said, although he missed out on being in the film.
"When we need a player we just go and get one from another band," said Hirst. "We can do that because we are the best."
GRIMETHORPE BAND REAPS PROFITS OF FILM FAME
The band's surge of popularity has given it even more muscle. It can command good fees for its frequent television appearances and can take its pick from the country's top brass musicians.

Unsurprisingly, Grimethorpe's good fortune has been eyed with envy and not a little bitterness by the rival brass bands with whom it competes ferociously each year in an endless round of national and international competitions.

In fact Grimethorpe only won second place in the national championships late last year, although to its great relief it beat its hottest foe, the Black Dyke Mills band, into third place. The winner was CWS Glasgow.
"We've been told we've set the brass band movement back 50 years because of all the swearing (in the film)," said conductor Peter Parkes, a grin betraying his delight at the controversy.

The band gathers for its regular Monday night practice session in a chilly room in the old National Coal Board headquarters on Grimethorpe's high street, which has been converted into a community centre.

It is the best-kept building on the street and it was just too slick for the makers of "Brassed Off". Instead they found a shabby room at the back of the local pub to film the band's practice sessions.
But Hirst fears that the band's good fortune could be short-lived. When "Brassed Off" has been forgotten the television fees will dry up and sponsorship may be harder to come by.
And there is a growing shortage of young players to make up the bands of the future.
"People used to learn to play their instruments at school, but with all the (government) spending cutbacks, music is one of the first things to go," said Hirst sadly.
